member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphFieldHash
member.summary: The name hash a GraphStream addresses its fields by — 0x4F9E70. Field names appear nowhere in a graph<n>.dat; only this hash does.

remarks.para: The hash is a weighted sum of the upper-cased characters: character k is multiplied by 1 + 317k and the products are added. The multiplier is kept in sixteen bits and wraps, so it repeats every 207 characters; no shipped field name is remotely long enough to reach that.
Case is folded by subtracting 32 from a–z only, so a name containing any other lower-case-adjacent byte hashes as written. Every shipped name is plain ASCII.

A collision is fatal at registration, not at read time: 0x4F9DF0 prints "GraphStream - collision in hash for %s" when a second field hashes to a value already registered. That is why the reader can treat the hash as an identity.

member.summary: The amount the per-character multiplier advances by, kept to sixteen bits.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphFile
member.summary: A MISSION:graphs/graph<n>.dat — an AI navigation graph and its precomputed route table.

remarks.para: Decoded from the loader at 0x4F9FF0 and the eleven field handlers the Graph and AIGraph registrars install (0x4FAA60, 0x508F80). The <n> is the id of the task that loads it (0x4FAE50 formats the name from it), which is why a level's graph numbers are scattered — level 1 ships 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 4019.

Two variants, told apart by the first four bytes. With the magic the file is a stream of named fields, each addressed by ; without it the loader rewinds and reads the same values positionally in a fixed order (0x4FA160). 293 of the 300 retail files are named; the seven positional ones are all in level 8.

Nothing in the file marks where a node ends. The engine stages fields into one buffer and commits a node when its nNodeCriteria arrives and a link when its eLinkType arrives; an nNodeID clears the staging buffer and an nLinkID1 resets both link ids to -1. That is the whole record structure, and it is reproduced here field for field rather than assumed to be a fixed group — a file that omitted, reordered or repeated a field would behave the same way as in the original.
The record order is uniform across the corpus all the same: nMaxNodes, RouteTable, then every node, then every link. 203 files have links and 90 have none.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphNearestNode
member.summary: Finds the graph node nearest a world position — 0x5096F0.

remarks.para: This is how a guard turns a position into somewhere on the graph. It is a linear scan of every slot with no spatial index, which is affordable because a graph holds at most a few hundred nodes and the query is not per-tick.
Three details that are not obvious:

list.item: nodes carrying are skipped entirely, so an observation post can never be the answer;

the engine keeps the best three in an insertion-sorted array and then returns only the first. The other two are computed and discarded. They are exposed here because a discarded computation that precise is a lead, not noise.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphNode
member.summary: One nav-graph node, as 0x4F9510 builds it.

remarks.para: The node lives in a flat array indexed by , so the array is as long as the file's nMaxNodes and mostly empty — level 1's first graph declares 100 slots and fills one. The engine's record is 576 bytes, of which the fields here occupy the first 52 plus the criteria string; the rest is runtime state (a 256-byte scratch area, the owning graph, the resolved material).

Three guards on creation, all reproduced by : an id of 1000 or more is silently dropped, an id past the current capacity grows the array, and a duplicate id is fatal ("GRAPHNODE ID ALREADY USED" followed by a hang). The largest id in the retail corpus is 380, so the cap is never approached.
Ids start at 1, not 0. Slot 0 is never occupied in any of the 300 retail graphs, and the nearest-node query walks slots from 0 and simply finds nothing there.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphNodeCriteria
member.summary: What a nav-graph node is for, as a bit set. A node's criteria is stored in the file as the constant's name; the engine resolves that name to a bit at load time.

remarks.para: The values are not written down anywhere in the binary. 0x5186C0 registers a criteria name into the next free slot of a 32-entry table and returns 1 << slot, so the numbering is registration order. AIGraph's registrar (0x508F80) registers DOOR, then VIEW, then STAIR — giving 1, 2, 4.

Because it is a bit set, a node could in principle carry several. None does: the file stores a single name, and across all 300 retail graphs only four values occur — the empty string 7022 times, NODECRITERIA_STAIR 669, NODECRITERIA_DOOR 465 and NODECRITERIA_VIEW 161.

is the one the engine tests on a hot path: the nearest-node query (0x5096F0) skips every node carrying it, so a view node can never be chosen as the start or end of a walk. They are observation posts, not path nodes.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphPositionalNodeExtras
member.summary: The two pieces of per-node data only the positional variant of a graph file carries, both of which the original reads and throws away.
member.param: The node these belong to.

An optional single-precision value between the radius and the material. Present when the next tag is . 0x4FA160 reads it into a local that it then reuses as a link id, so the value never reaches the node.
The first of the hook's two counted lists of integer pairs.
The second.

remarks.para: The lists come from 0x509480, the per-node message the positional loader sends the graph's own class so a subclass can read its own data inline. AIGraph's handler reads {count, count × (i32, i32)} twice and stores none of it — both integers of every pair go into the same local. So this is data the shipped engine parses only to advance the cursor.

It is not always empty: of the 130 positional nodes in the retail corpus, 41 carry at least one pair, with list lengths up to three. Retained here rather than skipped, because a format this thoroughly discarded is exactly the kind a mod or a level editor would put meaning back into.

Whether is present is a property of the file, not the node: of the seven positional files, six have it on every node and one (level 8's graph22.dat, 65 nodes) on none. That reads as two exporter versions rather than an optional field.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphRouteTable
member.summary: The precomputed all-pairs route table an AIGraph carries. There is no runtime A* — a walk is a table lookup per step.

remarks.para: The table is nMaxNodes² entries of eight bytes, {i32 nextNode, f32 cost}, allocated and filled with the sentinel by 0x5092E0/0x509340 and then overwritten wholesale from the file's RouteTable blob.

The indexing is from + to × maxNodes — column-major, the destination being the major axis (0x509390). Getting this backwards is not a crash: the table stays in range and reads plausibly, it just returns a node that is nowhere near the walker. With the right order the entry's node is a direct neighbour of the node being walked from in 1088822 of 1088822 reachable retail pairs; with the transpose it is one in 5.8% of them, which is what caught the mistake.

is {-1, -1.0f} and means "no route". It fills the diagonal (a node has no route to itself — all 8317 of them), every slot whose endpoints are not both occupied (all 3237161 of them), and 5700 genuinely unreachable live pairs.
The cost is in engine units and strictly decreases along a route — verified for all 1039956 interior steps in the corpus, which is what guarantees terminates without needing a visited set.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphStreamReader
member.summary: The tagged-value reader a graph<n>.dat is built from — the engine's own "GraphStream".

remarks.para: Every value in the stream is tagged: one byte naming a , then the payload. Nothing else delimits anything. A field is three consecutive tagged values — its name hash, its declared type, and its data — which is why an unknown field can be skipped by consuming exactly two of them (0x4FA3B0 called with a count of 2).

The tag on the payload is never checked. Each reader in 0x4F9CD0's dispatch is chosen by the field's declared type and then reads a fixed number of bytes, discarding the first. So a stream whose payload tag disagrees with its declared type is read as the declared type, silently. The peek at 0x4FAA10 looks like the missing check but is not one: it reads the tag and immediately seeks back one byte, and 0x4F9CD0 throws its return value away. Its one real use is the positional variant, which peeks to decide whether an optional field is present at all.
This reader keeps the same shape — does not consume — and additionally exposes the payload tag it skipped so a caller can assert the two agree. Retail data always agrees; the corpus test pins that.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphStreamReader.SkipValue
member.summary: Skips one tagged value of any type, using only its tag to find its width.

remarks.para: This is 0x4FA3B0's body for a single value. An unrecognised tag advances by nothing but the tag byte — the original's switch has no default arm — so a corrupt stream walks forward one byte at a time rather than stopping. Reproduced, because it is what decides whether a damaged file loads at all.

The blob arm disagrees with , in the original as much as here. Skipping expects {tag, u32 length, payload}; reading expects {tagged element type, tagged length, payload}, which is two bytes longer and starts with the element type's tag rather than a one. So skipping an unknown field whose data is a blob desynchronises the stream. It cannot happen on retail data — every field name in all 300 files is one of the eleven registered ones, which the corpus test asserts — but it is an inconsistency in the original, not a simplification here.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ai.GraphValueType
member.summary: The eleven value kinds a GraphStream tag can carry. The code is stored twice for every field — once as the field's declared type and once as the tag on the payload itself.

remarks.para: The numbering is fixed by the skip routine at 0x4FA3B0, which is the only place in the engine that maps every code to a width without knowing what the field means. The reader dispatch at 0x4F9CD0 agrees with it and adds the interpretation.

Codes come in pairs that share a width — 0/1, 2/3, 4/5 — which is how a signed and an unsigned form of the same width are told apart. shares its width with the 32-bit integers, so 4, 5 and 6 all skip four bytes.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneClip
member.summary: One clip playing on a bone object — a clock over a , and the rotations it yields for every bone that inherits it.

remarks.para: The original's clip instance is built by 0x4D47D0, which registers a five-field record { advance, sample, tick, callback, context } — 0x4D4840, 0x4D5180, 0x4D4B60 and 0x4D5080. This is those first three; the fourth, the clip's completion callback, is not read.

The important part is which track a bone reads. 0x4D5180 indexes the animation's rotation tracks by the asking node's own bone index, not by the bone the clip was started on — which is why one clip started on the root drives a whole skeleton. See .

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneClip.ArmStartEvents
member.summary: Makes the next also report events lying exactly at the clock's start.

remarks.para: This is clip flag 0x8000, which 0x4D47D0 sets on every clip node it creates. On the first tick 0x4D4B60 sees it and, before the ordinary interval, dispatches a point query at the old clock — the only way an event authored at a clip's very start can fire, since a forward interval is open there. The tick then clears it.

It is armed by the caller rather than by the constructor: the rule is global in the original, but only the traversal clips have been checked against it here. Walk cycles carry their first footstep at time zero as well, and arming those changes when a guard's first step is heard.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneClip.Tick
member.summary: Advances the clock by one tick.

remarks.para: Transcribed from 0x4D4B60:

A looping clip adjusts by one duration rather than taking a remainder, so a rate longer than the clip can leave the clock beyond the other end — the original does not guard that and neither does this. exposes the same interval-based event crossing used by the retail ladder state machine.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneClip.CrossedEvent(System.Int32)
member.summary: Tests whether the last tick crossed an authored event of the requested type.
member.param: The event id stored in the animation.
member.returns: when the event lies in the interval advanced last tick.
member.remarks: The interval is open at the old clock and closed at the new one. Consequently a ladder clip held at its time-zero boundary does not repeatedly fire that boundary, while wrapping through zero does fire it once. Reverse playback uses the mirrored rule.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneClip.TryGetCrossedEvent(System.Int32,System.Single@)
member.summary: Finds the first event of a type the last tick dispatched, and the time it is authored at.
member.param: The event id stored in the animation.
Receives the event's authored time.
member.returns: when such an event was crossed.
member.remarks: "First" is the original's order: 0x4D4DC0 walks the events in stored order, and a wrapping tick dispatches the part before the seam before the part after it. The time matters to the ladder states, which latch it (Human+3464) and ignore a crossing of the time they last took.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneClip.HasEventAtCurrentTime(System.Int32)
member.summary: Whether an event of the type is authored exactly where the clock stands.
member.param: The event id stored in the animation.
member.returns: when such an event sits at the current time.
member.remarks: A clip started this tick has no interval yet, but the original's point query on a new node (flag 0x8000, 0x4D4B60) dispatches what is authored at its start -- a walk cycle's first footstep.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneClip.UpcomingEvent(System.Int32)
member.summary: Whether the clock's next step will cross an event of the type -- the interval the original has already dispatched when this clock stands where it does.
member.param: The event id stored in the animation.
member.returns: when such an event lies in (time, time + rate], wrapping as a looping clip does.
member.remarks: The original advances a clip on the tick the clip is started, with a point query at its start (flag 0x8000), and drops that first step's root motion; this clock starts a step later and samples its root motion a step ahead, so the two travel identically while this clock reads one step behind. Probed on mission 4: patrol 411's walk (clip 57) read 160 on the original after the tick it set off, 0 here, at the same position, and its footsteps fell on ticks 1, 17, 34 where reading the interval behind gave 2, 18, 35.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneClip.SkipTo(System.Single)
member.summary: Moves the clock, without advancing it.
member.param: Where to start.
member.remarks: sub_4D65B0, which writes the clip's +44 — the clock steps and compares against the duration. The rate lives at +40 and a different function sets it, so this changes where a clip plays from and never how fast. Its one retail caller is the timed fire action, which starts each shot's animation at a random point.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneObject
member.summary: A skeleton instance: one node per bone, each able to carry an orientation source, and the pose those sources produce.

remarks.para: This is the original's bone object — the thing 0x4D2D60 builds and every drawable carries inline at its +104. Its palette is 132 bytes a bone; the fields this reproduces are the source pointer at +128, the propagate flag 0x20000 in the flag word at +4, and the world position and rotation at +24 and +36 that fills.

A source is inherited. A node with none of its own uses whatever came down from above, and a node's own source only reaches its children when its 0x20000 flag is set — which 0x4D61D0 sets on every node it starts a clip on. That is how one clip started on bone 0 drives a whole skeleton without a per-bone binding.

Blending. The original wraps a started clip in a blend node ({ i32 type, void *child } slots, -1 empty / 0 blend / 1 clip) and cross-fades two branches with a weight from a callback on the node (0x4D5EC0, 0x4D5FF0). 0x4D61D0 takes the immediate path — replacing the source outright — only when the blend time is under a tick; otherwise it eases from the old source to the new over that time. reproduces both: with no blend time (the default) it replaces, and with one it ramps a weight 0 → 1 over blendSeconds × 4800 / 160 ticks and slerps the outgoing and incoming poses at that weight. The blend node's full recursive tree is flattened here to one outgoing branch per bone, which is all a whole-rig cross-fade (a clip on bone 0 driving every bone) needs.

remarks.para: The engine's own orientation source, generalised. sub_4D6130 attaches a bone to a node that combines a clip with a stored orientation, and sub_4D5820's type 5 resolves that node as stored ⊗ sampled — the stored rotation on the left, which is what puts it in the parent's frame rather than the bone's own. This composes on the same side for the same reason: bending a spine means turning it where it joins the pelvis, not where it joins its own child.
A bend moves the bone's descendants and not the bone itself, because a bone is placed by its parent's rotation () — which is exactly what a joint does.

How long to cross-fade from whatever was playing on the bone into the new clip. Zero (the default) replaces the source outright; a value that works out to a tick or more eases into it. This is 0x4D61D0's a5, converted to ticks with the same × 4800 / 160 the original uses.

member.summary: Samples the root-motion track of the clip attached to bone 0.
member.returns: The root's position at the current time, or zero when bone 0 has no source.

remarks.para: 0x4D2FB0, reached from every consumer as (out position, out delta, boneObject). It looks at the root node's own source — boneObject[2] + 128, not an inherited one — and asks it for both, through the clip's advance callback 0x4D4840.

This is not only locomotion. On the first-person rig it is the weapon's hold offset: every weapon's standing clip carries a translation track whose value is where that weapon sits relative to the eye, and 0x464BD0 commits the view object's position as eye + orientation · thisValue. Dropping it puts every weapon in the middle of the screen.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneObject.BlendedRootMotionDelta
member.summary: The root's step over the last tick with a cross-fade mixed in, BoneBlend_GetMotion (0x4D3020).
member.returns: The per-tick root-motion delta, in engine units.
member.remarks: While a clip fades in over another, the root's step is the two clips' steps mixed by the fade's weight as it stood when the tick began: none of the new clip's on the tick it was started, a sixth of it the next on a six-tick fade, and all of it once the fade is done. So a run started from a stand gathers pace over the blend instead of leaving at full stride.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneRotationSampler
member.summary: Samples a bone's rotation track at a time, reproducing 0x4D5180.

remarks.para: Linear mode is a plain slerp between the two bracketing keys. Spline mode is SQUAD — the key slerp and the tangent slerp, blended by 2s(1-s) — with the keys' stored tangent quaternions as the quadrangle control points.

The original reads each segment's angle and 1/sin(angle) out of a table baked onto the track record, and encodes "negate the target quaternion" by storing the angle plus a full turn. Nothing read so far builds that table, so this computes the same quantities from the two quaternions; the branch structure and the thresholds are the original's.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.Igi2AnimationClip
member.summary: One I.G.I. 2 animation clip: an ILFF MINA form, one file per clip, under anims/.

remarks.para: The sequel replaced I.G.I. 1's per-skeleton animation sets with one file per clip, named by what it shows (anims/preripcord.iff, anims/stand_rifle_aim.iff), so a clip is found by name and carries its own bone hierarchy. Hierarchy_LoadAnim (igi2 0x57F060) reads four chunks:

item.description: The AnimHeader_s, used in place: version, loop flag, total time, bone count, event count, attach-object count and the clip's name. Pointer fields are written by the loader and ignored here.
The bone hierarchy, in the layout a bone mesh shares; see . Its shape is what matches the clip to a model.

A stream of variable-length records () in time order, ending in an end record — and then, after the end record, the tail: the keys that close a looping track, reachable only through the next link of the key before them. In a 9440-unit loop the last root key at 4800 links to a tail key at 9600 carrying key 0's value, which is how the track wraps. The header's event count includes the tail; across all 1,244 shipped clips it is exactly the stream records plus the tail records.
The attach objects, 80 bytes each, present in 1,090 of the 1,244 clips.

remarks.para: A key's next is a dword offset into the event chunk, which the loader turns into a pointer. Tracks are assembled by following those links from each track's first key, so a track is exactly the chain the engine interpolates along. Every link in the corpus lands on a record of the same track with a later time; this reader refuses a clip where one does not.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.Igi2BoneHierarchy
member.summary: An I.G.I. 2 bone hierarchy: the HIER chunk both a bone mesh and an animation clip carry.

remarks.para: One child-count byte per bone, padded to four bytes, then one real32x3 translation per bone. The bytes are the hierarchy's identity: Hierarchy_Register (igi2 0x57EDF0) keys its table on them, which is how a clip is matched to a model without either naming the other — a clip can drive any model whose hierarchy has the same shape ().

The two copies are not interchangeable. BoneDynCubeObj_SetLODVirModel (0x567BE0) takes the hierarchy, the bone count and the translations a posed bone is offset by from the mesh; a clip contributes only rotations and the root's motion. A clip's own translations are those of the rig it was authored on.

member.summary: Builds the shared skeleton this hierarchy describes.

member.remarks: The root's rest translation is zero whatever the chunk stores. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.Igi2ClipSampler
member.summary: Samples an the way the sequel's animation controller does.

remarks.para: AnimController_Step (igi2 0x5549A0) makes each key active once the controller's time reaches it, and AnimController_InterpolateHandler (0x5540F0) then blends every active key toward the key its next link names, at t = (time − key.time) / (next.time − key.time). A key with no next holds. So a track sampled before its first key reads nothing; the controller never asks, because every shipped track starts at time zero.

The result is local: a root translation and one rotation per bone, which is what composes into a posed skeleton — the same composition BoneDynCubeObj_UpdateHierarchy (0x564B50) performs, so both games share it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.Igi2ClipSampler.Slerp(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Quaternion32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Quaternion32,System.Double)
member.summary: The sequel's quaternion slerp, Quat32_SLERP (igi2 0x5635D0).
member.param: The orientation at t = 0.
The orientation at t = 1.
The parameter.

remarks.para: Not I.G.I. 1's slerp, and the differences are behaviour rather than style:

item.description: The angle is √(1 − d)·(((−0.0187293·d + 0.0742610)·d − 0.2121144)·d + 1.5707288) — the polynomial arc-cosine, not a library one.
The cut-over to a plain lerp is on the dot product, above , and the lerp is not renormalised.
The shorter arc is taken by negating the start weight when the dot is negative; below −0.99999 it lerps toward the negated end instead.

remarks.para: The original passes the end in ecx and the start in edx; this takes them in reading order. Arithmetic is done in double precision, as the x87 stack the original runs on does it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.CollisionLayout
member.summary: How a title lays out a model's collision geometry.
member.param: Bytes per collision face.
Bytes per collision vertex.
Bytes per collision material row.
Bytes per node of the sphere tree.
Where a material row keeps its portal index.
Where a material row keeps the global game-material row.

remarks.para: Read out of the sequel's own symbols rather than measured, because two of these are the kind of difference that produces a wrong answer instead of a failure. MultiMesh_Face_t is 12 bytes there — aiVertex[3], iMaterial, then an iLightmap and a pad — where Project I.G.I.'s face is 8; and MultiMesh_Material_t is 16 where the first game's is 12, having gained iBumpMap and iEnvMap at offsets 8 and 10.

That second one moves a field rather than appending one. The global game-material row — which is what tells the sight test glass from a wall — sits at offset 8 in the first game and at 12 in the sequel, because the two new fields were inserted before it rather than after. A reader that only widened the stride would keep reading offset 8 and get the bump-map index, which is a small number indexing a real table and would look entirely plausible.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.AssetFormatProfile
member.summary: Which encodings of each asset format one game title ships.

remarks.para: Readers parse what the bytes say; this says which bytes a title is allowed to have said. That is the original's own separation — Texture_LoadFile (0x4B24C0) rejects an unexpected version in the loader and the header parser downstream never sees a bad one — and keeping it means a file from the wrong game fails loudly instead of half-loading into something that looks nearly right.

The two titles overlap more than expected, so this is mostly a correctness seam rather than an enabler. Measured against a retail installation of each: I.G.I. 2's textures are all version 11 and its sprites all version 9, both of which the readers already parse. Models are where they differ: I.G.I. 1 ships mesh version 0.10 and I.G.I. 2 ships 0.16, and their render headers are different sizes — see .
I.G.I. 1's sets are what its readers have always accepted, not a re-measurement, so introducing this cannot narrow what already loads.

member.remarks: Both titles emit 8, checked across every .qvm in a retail installation of each. It is carried anyway because it is the field that would tell us a build had changed instruction set, and finding that out from a garbled disassembly would be much worse than reading it here.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Formats.AssetFormatProfile.MeshRenderHeaders
member.summary: Gets where the counts sit in a model's render header, per mesh format.
member.remarks:
The one place the two games' model format genuinely differs, and it differs less than it first appears: only the size changes. I.G.I. 2's trailing runtime binding block is shorter — 36, 40 and 44 bytes against 48, 56 and 56 — and every field sits where I.G.I. 1 puts it.
The skinned layout is the one to be careful with. Its vertex count at offset 20 is the total rows in the vertex chunk, base vertices plus extra influences; the mesh header's own count is the base alone. Matching the header's dwords against that count picks offset 16 and then fails on every skinned model, which is how this was got wrong once already.

remarks.para: A .olm entry is a 60-byte prefix, then one descriptor per image, then the pixel blocks in the same order at four bytes a texel. Only the descriptor differs between the games: I.G.I. 2's carries two more dwords than I.G.I. 1's, 52 against 44.

The dimensions are always the descriptor's last dword, so they move with it and this one number is enough. That is not a coincidence of two layouts — it is how the writer builds the record, appending the size beside the pixel pointer it clears.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Formats.AssetFormatProfile.MeshHeaderCountsBaseVertices
member.summary: Gets whether a mesh header's vertex count is the base count rather than the total.

remarks.para: A skinned model's vertex chunk holds its base vertices followed by the extra weighted influences that accumulate into them, and the render header carries both counts and their sum. What the mesh header holds differs between the games: I.G.I. 1 puts the total there and I.G.I. 2 puts the base.

Measured across 2,048 models from ten retail I.G.I. 2 archives: all 101 skinned models carry the base count, and in both games the base and the extras sum to the total and the vertex chunk holds exactly that many rows. For unskinned models there is no difference, because the two are equal.
means "either" — for a tool reading a file without knowing which game it came from, where the cross-check is not available rather than satisfied.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ilff.IlffContainer
member.summary: A parsed ILFF container: the archive format behind .res, .mef and .fnt files.

remarks.para: Parsing is zero-copy. The container keeps a view of its own bytes, and every chunk payload is a slice of that view.
The layout is documented in docs/formats/ilff.md. Two rules matter more than the rest:

item.description: The header's size field is the total container size, header included — verified against retail archives, where it equals the file length exactly.

A chunk's payload starts at alignUp(chunkOffsetInParent + 16, chunk.align), where the offset is measured from the parent container's base — not from the start of the file and not from the chunk. For a nested container the base moves, so the same chunk bytes align differently.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ilff.IresIndex
member.summary: Lists what an IRES archive holds and where, without reading any of it.

remarks.para: needs the whole file in memory, which is right for the game's own archives — the largest is 15 MB and its entries are handed out as slices of that one buffer. It is wrong for an overrides archive. Replacement art is BGRA8 at four times the size, so a level's archive can pass a quarter of a gigabyte, and the override index has to walk EVERY archive in the folder on every rescan just to learn which names it carries.

So this walks the chunk list over a , reading the 16-byte headers and the short NAME payloads and seeking past everything else. What comes back is where each entry's bytes are, not the bytes: the caller reads the slice it actually wants, when it wants it.
The layout it walks is the one documents, with the same per-chunk alignment rule writes.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Ilff.IresWriter
member.summary: Builds an ILFF+IRES archive: the .res files the game loads its resources from.

remarks.para: The counterpart to , and written to the same description: a stream of NAME chunks, each followed by the payload chunks it names.

ALIGNMENT IS PER CHUNK, not per archive, and that is the one rule it is easy to get wrong because 91 of the game's 92 archives hide it — they align everything to 4, so nothing distinguishes the chunk's alignment from the container's. The 92nd, common/textures/common.res, aligns its container and every BODY to 32 while leaving each NAME at 4. A writer that assumes one number for the whole file reproduces that archive 7,776 bytes too long.

So: a payload sits at alignUp(chunkOffset + 16, chunkAlign), and a chunk advances by alignUp(payloadEnd, chunkAlign) - chunkOffset, with zero on the last one to end the walk. MEASURED: with that rule every one of the retail archives rebuilds from its own entries byte for byte, alignment 32 included.

The one thing the retail files disagree with each other about is the FINAL chunk: 61 pad it out to its alignment and 31 stop at the last payload byte. Both read back the same, so this pads, and the difference is at most a few bytes on the end of a file.

ENTRY ORDER IS PRESERVED, and it is not cosmetic. The original hashes names into one table where the FIRST registration wins, so an archive holding a name twice resolves to whichever copy came first. Rebuilding in a different order therefore changes which picture a name means, which is invisible at every later stage because both copies decode perfectly well.
Names are written back exactly as they were read, LOCAL: namespace prefix included. The prefix is part of the name the game looks a resource up by, not decoration on the path.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Formats.Ilff.IresWriter.DefaultAlignment
member.summary: The alignment 91 of the game's 92 archives use, and the default for a new one.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Formats.Ilff.IresWriter.NameAlignment
member.summary: The alignment every NAME chunk uses, whatever the archive aligns its payloads to.
member.remarks: Four in every retail archive, including the one that aligns its bodies to 32. A name is a short string and there is nothing to gain by padding it out to a cache line.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Legacy.FlatResourceArchive
member.summary: The flat "RESOURCE" archive: the second container shape the original's resource registrar recognises.

remarks.para: Res_Register (0x4B5F80) dispatches on the first bytes of a buffer: ILFF selects the path, the ASCII text RESOURCE selects this one, and anything else is registered as a single opaque blob.

Inferred, not confirmed. No retail file uses this layout — it looks like a development-only format — so the record layout comes from reading the original's parser rather than from real bytes. Treat a parse failure here as a reason to re-read 0x4B5F80, not as corrupt data.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.IlsfAdpcmDecoder
member.summary: Expands the four-bit ADPCM the and forms carry into signed 16-bit PCM.

remarks.para: Transcribed from the original decoder 0x496280 and its state initialiser 0x496420. The scheme is plain IMA/DVI ADPCM: the index table at 0x543920 is {-1,-1,-1,-1,2,4,6,8} repeated for the signed half, and the 89-entry step table at 0x543930 is the standard one, both verified byte-for-byte against the image.

Two details are not obvious from the tables and cost a channel swap or a click if missed. Nibbles are taken high first within a byte, and channels interleave per sample, not per block — a stereo frame is one byte holding left in the high nibble and right in the low. The original keeps one predictor and one step index per channel and at most two channels fit its state record, so this decoder enforces the same bound.

Divergence, deliberate: the original does not store the half-consumed byte across calls. It sets a flag and expects the caller to re-present that byte at the head of the next buffer, which the resident path never exercises because it decodes in one call. This decoder holds the byte itself, so a streaming caller can hand it strictly forward-moving buffers. The samples produced are identical.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.IlsfFormat
member.summary: How an ILSF sound stores its samples, and whether the original kept it resident.

remarks.para: The four codes are the arms of the switch in the original loader 0x495F70, and they form a two-bit pair: bit 0 selects resident over streamed, bit 1 selects ADPCM over raw PCM. The loader treats them as follows — a streamed sound keeps only its file name (record +40) and never allocates or fills a sound buffer, a resident PCM sound points straight at the payload in place, and a resident ADPCM sound allocates the decoded size and expands through 0x496280 before the buffer is filled and the temporary is freed.

The distinction is a runtime policy rather than a difference in the bytes: both streamed codes decode exactly like their resident counterparts. All four codes ship, and a census of a retail installation shows the split is exactly where the reading predicts — no streamed sound lives inside an archive, because a streamed sound is only a file name and must stay reopenable.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.IlsfHeader
member.summary: The twenty-byte header every ILSF sound starts with, parsed on its own so a streaming reader can learn a sound's shape without touching its payload.

remarks.para: Read from the original loader 0x495F70, which copies these twenty bytes verbatim into its forty-eight-byte runtime record at +16 and drives everything else off them. Layout:
remarks.code: +0 char[4] "ILSF" +4 u16 format — see IlsfFormat +6 u16 bitsPerSample — the *decoded* width; 16 for every shipped sound +8 u16 channels — 1 or 2 +10 u16 reserved — zero in every shipped file +12 u32 sampleRate — mostly 22050, but 44100 and 11025 also ship +16 u32 frameCount — samples per channel, not bytes
remarks.para: frameCount counting frames rather than bytes is worth stating, because the header gives no payload length and the two readings differ by the block size. Measurement settles it: m1_ambience.wav (streamed PCM, stereo) has a payload of exactly frameCount * 4 bytes, and game_music.wav (streamed ADPCM, stereo) exactly frameCount bytes, which is the one byte per stereo frame that four-bit ADPCM produces.

member.summary: The size in bytes of an ILSF header.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.IlsfHeader.RetailSampleRate
member.summary: The rate the original's output runs at: Snd_Init 0x4952F0 sets the primary buffer to 22050 Hz.
member.remarks: It is not the rate of every shipped sound. A census of the 759 sounds in a retail installation finds 678 at 22050, 69 at 44100 and 12 at 11025 — the original simply lets DirectSound resample a secondary buffer into the primary. Nothing may assume a single rate.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.IlsfStreamReader
member.summary: Pulls 16-bit PCM out of an ILSF sound a slice at a time, without ever holding the whole sound in memory.

remarks.para: This is the path the and forms exist for. The original kept only the file name for those two codes (loader 0x495F70, record +40) precisely so the long sounds — the music track and the ambience beds — would not sit in memory: a retail music track is three megabytes packed and about thirteen expanded.
Samples come out as 16-bit whatever the file declares. Nothing in retail is 8-bit, but the header allows it and widening here keeps every caller on one sample type.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.MpegAudioHeader
member.summary: The four-byte frame header an MPEG audio stream starts every frame with, parsed on its own so the sound bank can learn a track's shape without decoding a sample of it.

remarks.para: Why the port needs this at all. Every sound in I.G.I. 1 is ILSF, and so is almost every sound in I.G.I. 2 — but not its music. The sequel's menu theme ships as menusystem/sound/menu_music.mp3 inside menusystem/sound/sounds.res, a 320 kbps MPEG-1 Layer III stream, and its mission scores ship as loose *_music.mp3 files beside each level. Retail decodes them through Miles (mss32.dll, shipped in the installation's pc directory); the port decodes them with a managed decoder behind .
The layout is ISO/IEC 11172-3 §2.4.1.3 and its MPEG-2 and MPEG-2.5 extensions, read big-endian:
remarks.code: 31..21 sync — eleven set bits 20..19 version — 00 MPEG-2.5, 01 reserved, 10 MPEG-2, 11 MPEG-1 18..17 layer — 00 reserved, 01 Layer III, 10 Layer II, 11 Layer I 16 protection — zero when a 16-bit CRC follows the header 15..12 bitrate index — 0 is "free", 15 is invalid 11..10 sample rate — 3 is reserved 9 padding — one extra slot in this frame 8 private 7..6 channel mode — 00 stereo, 01 joint stereo, 10 dual channel, 11 mono
remarks.para: Only the first frame is read. That is enough for the rate, the channel count and — for the constant bitrate every retail track uses — a duration, and it keeps mounting an archive cheap: a scan for the true length would have to walk all eight megabytes of the menu theme.

member.summary: Pulls 16-bit PCM out of an MPEG audio stream a slice at a time, without ever holding the decoded sound in memory.

remarks.para: The counterpart of for I.G.I. 2's music, and it streams for the same reason: the sequel's menu theme is three and a half minutes of 320 kbps stereo — eight megabytes packed and about thirty-six expanded — and retail never holds either, because Miles decodes it a buffer at a time behind mss32.dll.
Samples come out as 16-bit whatever the stream's internal precision, so every caller stays on one sample type and the audio layer needs to know nothing about which of the two formats it is hearing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.MpegAudioStreamReader.ReadFrames(System.Span{System.Int16})
member.summary: Reads the next frames into .
member.param: Receives channel-interleaved 16-bit samples.
member.returns: The number of frames written, or zero at the end of the stream.

remarks.para: The destination is filled, not merely written to. A decoder produces whole granules — 1152 frames at a time for Layer III — and a caller asks for whatever its buffer holds, so the two never line up. What is decoded past the end of one call is kept and served to the next rather than dropped, which is what lets this answer a small buffer at all.

That matters more than it sounds. The device's fill loop reads until its buffer is full and treats a zero as the end of the sound — so a reader that returned zero with samples still to come would have a looping track rewind, read zero again, and rewind again: a hang rather than a glitch. Returning zero here means the stream really is exhausted.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.MpegAudioStreamReader.Restart
member.summary: Rewinds to the first frame so the sound can loop.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Sound.MpegAudioStreamReader.Decode
member.summary: Pulls the next chunk out of the decoder into the pending buffer.
member.remarks: The request is four bytes per sample rather than two, and deliberately: NLayer sizes its output from the buffer as though it held 32-bit samples and then writes 16-bit ones, so it fills half of whatever it is given. Asking for double gets a full chunk in one call, and a buffer that big is safe either way — a decoder that filled the whole request would still be within it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Sprites.SpriteLoader.ReadTileLayout(System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.Int32,System.Int32,System.String)
member.summary: Reads the trailing "LOOP" version 6 tile-grid block a picture's header points at. Mirrors TileGrid_Load (0x4B75C0).

remarks.para: Block layout: the magic and version, two words at +8 and +12, the column and row counts at +16 and +20, then a 16-byte record per cell holding { reserved, x, y, frameNumber }.

The original reads exactly two things — the column and row counts, and the low byte of each record's frame number — and derives every tile's position from its grid cell. So the per-record x and y are redundant, and the two words at +8/+12 are not read at all: in the large pictures they happen to hold the picture's size, but in pointer.spr and the window-frame sprites they hold stale pointer values. Reading them would work on the files that made the theory look right and produce nonsense on the rest.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Sprites.SpriteTileLayout
member.summary: The tile grid that reassembles a large picture from a sprite's frames.

remarks.para: Pictures larger than a texture the hardware of the day could hold are stored as a grid of tiles — mainmenu.pic is 150 frames of 64×32 laid out ten across and fifteen down, which is exactly 640×480. The grid lives in a trailing "LOOP" version 6 block that the sprite header points at, and the original parses it in TileGrid_Load (0x4B75C0) into the same cell table a font's character map uses.
Cell values are one-based. A cell holds frameIndex + 1, and zero means "no tile". The same convention governs a font's character map; see .

The block also carries two words that look like a picture width and height, and for the large pictures they even hold plausible values — but the original never reads them, and in the small sprites they hold stale pointers left over from whatever wrote the file. They are not exposed here for that reason; the assembled size is Columns × tileWidth by Rows × tileHeight.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.AlphaCoverage
member.summary: Rescales the alpha of a mip chain so that an alpha-tested surface keeps the same amount of itself at every distance — alpha-to-coverage-preserving mipmaps (Castaño, 2010).

remarks.para: The problem this exists for. A chain-link fence is drawn as a flat quad with a texture whose alpha is the wire. Halving that texture averages neighbouring texels, and averaging a thin bright wire against a wide transparent gap gives something dimmer than the wire was. Do it five or six times and most of the wire's alpha has fallen below whatever cutoff the shader tests against — so the fence thins out with distance, and then flickers, because which texels survive the cutoff changes as the mip level crosses over. The far fence goes faint while the near one stays solid, and neither is what the artist drew.

The fix, and why it is a rescale rather than a better filter. No averaging filter can preserve a threshold test, because the test is not linear: what has to be preserved is the FRACTION OF TEXELS THAT PASS IT, and that is a property of the whole level rather than of any neighbourhood. So each level is filtered as usual and then its alpha is scaled by a single number chosen so that the fraction passing the cutoff matches the top level's. It is done once, when the texture is imported.

Why the scale is searched rather than computed. Coverage as a function of the scale is a step function — it only changes when some texel crosses the cutoff — so it cannot be inverted. It is monotonic, though, which is what makes a bisection both correct and quick.

member.summary: Rescales each mip level's alpha so the fraction of texels passing matches level zero's.
member.param: The whole mip chain, largest level first, modified in place.
Level zero's width in pixels.
Level zero's height in pixels.
How many levels the chain holds.
The alpha the shader tests against, as a 0..1 fraction.
member.returns: when the chain was alpha tested and levels were rescaled.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.AlphaCoverage.WidenCutout(System.Span{OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Bgra32},System.Single)
member.summary: Widens a cut-out texture's alpha so its partly-covered edge texels survive the shader's test.
member.param: The whole mip chain, modified in place.
The alpha the shader tests against, as a 0..1 fraction.
member.returns: when the texture was a cut-out and was widened.

remarks.para: The shader clips at a half, which throws away the partly-covered texels along the edge of every wire, slat and leaf. The difference is visible: clipped at essentially zero — every texel carrying any alpha at all drawn — barbed wire is perceptibly thicker against the same sky, and chain-link holds together at distances where a half-clip has thinned it to a haze.

Why this is not simply a lower cutoff. Lowering it for everything is catastrophic, and was measured to be: the game's window glass carries partial alpha as a genuine transparency, so a low cutoff turns a pane opaque and the office window falls from 156 to 38 out of 255. So the two cases have to be told apart, and the texture itself is what tells them apart: a cut-out's alpha is nearly all zero or nearly all full, with only edge texels in between, while glass lives in the middle band. Only the first kind is widened, and it is widened at load rather than in the shader — which needs no per-draw state, no seam change, and cannot affect a surface that was not classified.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.BitmapImage
member.summary: A Windows bitmap, decoded to .

remarks.para: Not an I.G.I. format. It is here because I.G.I. 2 stores its environment cube maps as plain .bmp files inside a resource archive and hands them to D3DXLoadSurfaceFromFileInMemory, which reads anything; this reader covers what the retail corpus actually ships and refuses the rest by name rather than silently producing the wrong pixels.

Supported: a BITMAPINFOHEADER with 24 or 32 bits per pixel and no compression, in either row order. All 186 cube-map faces in the retail tree are 24-bit BI_RGB with a 40-byte header and pixels at offset 54, so the 32-bit case is there because it costs one branch, not because anything needs it. Palettised, run-length encoded and bitfield bitmaps are refused.

Decoding to is free rather than a conversion: a bitmap row already stores blue, green and red in that order, which is the same layout the engine's textures and lightmaps use. A 24-bit source gets an opaque alpha, matching the D3DFMT_X8R8G8B8 surface the original loads it into.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.JpegImage
member.summary: A JPEG image, as I.G.I. 2 ships its terrain textures.

remarks.para: Nothing here reproduces game behaviour. I.G.I. 2 does not decode JPEG itself: Direct3DTexture_DownloadFromFile (igi2ed 0x662FE0) hands the raw bytes to D3DXCreateTextureFromFileInMemoryEx, and the shipped binary carries a statically linked libjpeg inside D3DX to do the work (?jpeg_read_header@D3DX@@, ?jpeg_start_decompress@D3DX@@). So the specification is the format's own, and correctness is measured against what any conforming decoder produces rather than against the original.

Progressive is not optional here. Of the 83 files the game ships, 68 are progressive and 15 baseline — so a baseline-only reader would decode fewer than a fifth of the ground's textures. Both are implemented, along with restart intervals, which 15 of the files use.

The corpus is 8-bit, three-component, and entirely 4:4:4 — no chroma subsampling anywhere. General sampling factors are still handled, with nearest-neighbour upsampling, because a reader that assumed the corpus's shape would fail on the first file that did not share it and would do so by producing a sheared image rather than an error.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.MipChainBuilder
member.summary: Builds the mip chain for a texture that shipped without one.

remarks.para: Most of this game's textures carry a single level. That was reasonable for the hardware it shipped on and is not reasonable now: a surface drawn smaller than its texture samples a scattering of unrelated texels, so it sparkles as the camera moves and every thin thing on it — a fence, a railing, a ladder — crawls. No amount of anisotropy fixes that; anisotropy chooses how many samples to take ALONG the footprint, and with one level there is nothing but the full-resolution texture to take them from. It is the missing levels that do the averaging.

Filtered in linear light. These textures are display-encoded, and averaging display-encoded values is averaging the wrong numbers — the mean of two encoded values is not the encoding of their mean. Doing it directly darkens every level a little more than the last, so a wall visibly changes tone with distance. Each level is therefore decoded, averaged, and re-encoded. Alpha is already linear and is averaged as it stands.

Colour is averaged weighted by alpha. A cut-out stores black or junk RGB wherever its alpha is zero, because nothing samples the colour of a hole — so a flat average lets those black gaps darken the wire's colour a level at a time, and the wire ends up passing the alpha test (coverage is restored) yet drawn black. Weighting each texel's colour by its own alpha keeps a transparent texel out of the colour sum entirely. An opaque texture, every alpha equal, is unaffected.
Coverage for alpha-tested surfaces is restored separately, by , once the chain exists — averaging is what costs the coverage, so it cannot be fixed while building.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.PackPicture
member.summary: The one container a generated pack writes: "LOOP" version 12.

remarks.para: Every picture in this game arrives in one of four shapes — a version 2 or 11 single texture, a version 7 or 9 multi-frame atlas — read by three different loaders that disagree about where the format code lives. Replacement art could be written back in each of those shapes, and the first plan was to do exactly that. This is better, for three reasons that only appeared once the whole corpus was in view.

Size. An upscale is BGRA8 at four times the width and height: 32 times the bytes of the A1R5G5B5 it replaces, which turns 120 MB of art into about 3 GB. The retail containers store raw rows and have nowhere to say otherwise. Here a frame is a PNG, which on this material is between three and five times smaller and costs a decode that the loader was already doing.

Layout must not follow resolution. The menu sizes the logo as grid.Columns * Frames[0].Width — the art's pixel count IS the layout — so a four-times picture would draw four times too big, and nothing in the retail formats can say otherwise because nothing needed to. So this records a LOGICAL size beside the real one, the loader reports the logical size as the frame's own, and a sharper menu is still a menu the same shape.

One writer instead of four. A sprite is not just pixels: it carries frame advances, offsets, a palette block and the tile grid that reassembles a 640x480 picture out of 150 frames of 64x32. Rewriting one in place means moving every block and fixing every pointer. Writing this instead means one layout to get right and one to test.
It is only ever written by the packer and only ever read from an overrides folder. Nothing in a retail installation is version 12, so a game with no pack never meets one.
THE LAYOUT. Little-endian throughout.
remarks.code:
header, 48 bytes 0x00 'LOOP' 0x04 version, 12 0x08 frame count, u32 0x0C flags, u32 bit 0: frames are PNG. bit 1: build a mip chain on load. bit 2: frames are block-compressed chains (see below) 0x10 logical width, u32 what a caller lays out with, whatever the pixels turned out to be 0x14 logical height, u32 0x18 grid columns, u32 0 when the picture is not a tile grid 0x1C grid rows, u32 0x20 grid cell offset, u32 columns*rows bytes of one-based frame numbers 0x24 three reserved dwords
frame table, 32 bytes each, immediately after the header 0x00 picture offset, u32 from the start of the file 0x04 picture length, u32 0x08 surface offset, u32 0 when the frame carries no derived map 0x0C surface length, u32 0x10 logical width, u16 NOT the pixel width; what layout uses 0x12 logical height, u16 0x14 advance, u16 0x16 offset x, i16 0x18 offset y, i16 0x1A reserved, u16 then u32
remarks.para: A BLOCK-COMPRESSED FRAME (bit 2, with bit 0 clear) holds a GPU-ready chain instead of a PNG. Its picture payload is a 32-byte header -- 'BCN1', format, width, height, levels, the offset and length of a small PNG proxy within the payload, and per-frame flags (bit 0: cut-out) -- then every level's blocks, largest first. The surface payload is the same shape with no proxy. Nothing is built at load: the chain was built, its cut-out widened and its coverage preserved when the pack was made.

THE SURFACE MAP IS ITS OWN SLOT, not a second frame, and that distinction is load-bearing. The arrangement it replaces put the picture in layer 0 and its packed normal-roughness-occlusion map in layer 1 of a multi-image container — which works only for as long as nothing else uses layer 1 for something else. A level's ground atlas is eighteen tiles in eighteen layers, and a sprite is its animation frames, so under that rule the second ground tile and the second frame of an explosion both read as somebody's normal map. Here a frame is always a picture and a map is always a map.

remarks.para: Why a pair and not a texture. A replacement asset in the overrides folder can hold its derived surface map as a second layer of the same file. Keeping them together is the point: they are produced together from the same source image and at the same resolution, so a format that lets them be installed separately is a format that lets them disagree — a normal map for a texture that has since been replaced is worse than no normal map at all, and nothing on screen would say which one is stale.
The game's own textures are single-image containers and always come back with no map, so a level made entirely of them behaves exactly as it did before any of this existed.

member.summary: A multi-image "LOOP" container — versions 7 and 9 — which stores a set of equally sized tiles rather than one texture with a mip chain.

remarks.para: A level's terrain/terrain.tex is one of these: eighteen 128×128 tiles that the terrain's tile maps index. deliberately refuses these versions, because a caller asking for "the texture" of an atlas has no sensible answer; this reads the whole set.

The 52-byte header is shared by both versions and the layer descriptors follow it directly. Version 7 gives every layer the file's own pixel mode and uses 40-byte descriptors; version 9 gives each layer its own mode and uses 32-byte ones. Retail terrain atlases are all version 9, mode .

The layer's mode is the sixth argument the original passes to its texture-create helper (0x4B23B0), which is the same position the .lmp path passes in — that is what identifies it as the format code rather than the file-level word at +0x12, which travels alongside as the secondary format.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.TextureDecoder
member.summary: Decodes a texture payload into pixels, one mip level at a time.

remarks.para: This is a transcription of the original's DownloadTexture (0x50AD90) and the four converters it dispatches to — 0x517FD0 (paletted), 0x517C90 (A1R5G5B5), 0x517F00 (32-bit copy) and 0x517DD0 (R5G6B5).

The channel order is the point of this class. Every converter writes blue to byte 0 and red to byte 2, and the 32-bit path performs no swizzle at all — so a 32-bit texture is stored on disk in exactly 's layout. Decoding through one type here means no backend has to guess.

member.param: The texture header describing the payload.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.TextureDescriptor
member.summary: Everything needed to decode a texture payload, normalised from the three different on-disk headers the original reads.

remarks.para: The original has three texture headers and they do not agree, which is why this type exists as a normalisation step rather than as a struct overlay:

item.description: A TEXH chunk (fonts, sprites) stores bits per pixel and derives the stride as allocatedWidth * bitsPerPixel / 8 — Texture_LoadFromIlff, 0x4B2070.

A .tex version 11 file has the same field order but stores bytes per pixel in the same slot and derives the stride as allocatedWidth * bytesPerPixel — Texture_LoadFile, 0x4B24C0. Reading it as a TEXH gives a stride eight times too small.
A .tex version 2 file has a shorter, differently ordered header that stores the stride directly and has no depth field at all.

member.summary: Wraps already-decoded pixels as a single-level texture.
member.param: The image width in pixels.

member.returns: The image as a texture with one level, ready to have a chain built onto it.
member.remarks: For pixels that came from somewhere other than a .tex — an upscaled replacement read off disk, a test fixture — so that everything downstream of the decode is reached by exactly one path. The correction sequence a texture needs (classify the cut-out, widen its alpha, build the chain, preserve its coverage) is load-bearing for every fence and canopy in the game, and a second entry point that skipped it would be a second, subtly different renderer.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.TextureImage.WithMipChain
member.summary: Returns this texture with a complete mip chain, building one if it shipped without.
member.returns: This instance when a chain already exists, otherwise a new image carrying one.
member.remarks: Most of this game's textures carry a single level, and a backend that generates none then samples full resolution at every distance -- which sparkles, and makes every fence and railing crawl. See for why anisotropy cannot stand in for the missing levels.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.TextureImage.RebuildMipChain
member.summary: Returns this texture with a freshly built mip chain, discarding any it shipped with.
member.returns: A new image whose chain was rebuilt from level zero.
member.remarks: keeps a chain a texture already carries, which is right for an opaque surface. A cut-out that shipped with a chain, though, carries the black of its transparent gaps in every level of it — the wire's colour was averaged flat against the holes at import — so it goes dark at distance no matter how well the alpha is preserved. Rebuilt from level zero, the alpha- weighted filter in keeps the wire's own colour instead. Build reads only level zero of the source, so a chain that is already present is simply replaced -- in place when the pixels have room for it, which changes this instance rather than copying it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.TexWriter
member.summary: Writes the "LOOP" containers and read.

remarks.para: The formats layer was read-only until replacement art needed somewhere to go. An overrides folder holds the game's own files, so anything that produces one has to write the game's own containers — and the only way to be confident about that is to write them beside the readers, with round-trip tests that decode what was encoded using the same code the game does.

ALWAYS , whatever the original was. The retail art is mostly A1R5G5B5: five bits a channel and one bit of alpha. Re-encoding to it would throw away most of what an upscale just produced — the banding in a 2001 sky is that format, not the resolution — and 32-bit costs bytes and nothing else, because every reader here decodes to anyway. It is the one format that is lossless by construction.
The version is chosen by the CALLER, not by this type, and that is deliberate: an override replaces one specific file, and a file the game opens as a version 2 texture has to come back as one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.Textures.TgaImage
member.summary: A Truevision TGA image, as I.G.I. 2 ships its sky, water and effect textures.

remarks.para: Nothing here reproduces game behaviour, and that is a finding rather than an omission. I.G.I. 2 does not decode these itself: Direct3DTexture_DownloadFromFile (igi2ed 0x662FE0) hands the raw file bytes to D3DXCreateTextureFromFileInMemoryEx, which sniffs the format and decodes it — the binary even carries a statically linked libjpeg inside D3DX for the other half. So there is no engine quirk to match: a standard-conformant reader is exactly right, and the format's own conventions are the specification.

A level names these files directly, with their own extension and alias — MISSION:textures/clouds1.tga — and they are loose files beside the level's archive rather than entries inside it. 84 such references appear across the shipped level scripts.

The retail corpus uses four shapes, none of them run-length encoded: 162 uncompressed 24-bit, 31 uncompressed 32-bit, 3 colour-mapped 8-bit and 1 greyscale. The run-length forms are decoded anyway, because they share the reader's tail and refusing a format the file says it is would be a worse failure than handling it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.Igi2ForestTree
member.summary: One tree placed by a forest_%d.dat file.
member.param: Where it stands, in world units.

Its orientation as the three angles Real32x9_Create builds a rotation matrix from, in radians. The third is the turn about the vertical that the forest task's Random rotation range scatters, and every tree in the corpus has one. The first two are the tilt onto the ground, and they are non-zero on exactly the trees whose stand has Normalize objects to ground set — nine stands, a quarter of the corpus.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.Igi2ForestData
member.summary: A level's forest_%d.dat: where every tree of one Forest task stands.

remarks.para: A length-prefixed header string followed by a bare array of fixed-size records, and nothing else — the file does not say how many trees it holds. The count comes from the task's Number of trees parameter, and Forest_LoadData (igi2.exe 0x59FBD0) lowers it to what the file can supply when the file is short. So the task is the authority and the file is the payload, the same way round as terrain; see .

The %d is the task's own level id — the slot it occupies in the level's 4096-entry Level_atLevelQTaskID table — not a parameter it declares. Forest_SaveData (0x59F980) finds it by scanning that table for the task, and Forest_UpdateInternalDataHandler (0x5A2F40) builds the same name to load it back.

There is no BSP tree in the file despite the format's own name for itself. Forest_CreateBSPTree (0x59F350) builds one from the tree array at load time, and the height data under it comes from Forest_GenerateHeightDataRecursively. The file is the placement and only the placement.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.Igi2TerrainMap
member.summary: One tile of I.G.I. 2 terrain data: a heightmap%03d.thm, .tmm or .tlm.

remarks.para: The three files are a set. TerrainMap_Alloc (igi2.exe 0x575030) loads all three by the same tile id, from heightmaps/heightmap%03d.ext, and substitutes a generated buffer for any one that is missing — so a tile with no .tlm is complete, not broken. All three normally arrive inside the ILFF archive heightmaps/heightmaps.res rather than as files on disk; the editor writes them loose and then bundles them, which is what TerrainMap_SaveHandler emits its temporary BeginResource/AddResource script for.

Each file is a fixed header followed by nWidth * nHeight samples in row-major order, with no padding and no per-row alignment. The engine takes the payload by pointer and uses it in place — pvHeightmap is float * at byte 52, piMaterialmap is unsigned char * at byte 44 and pbLightmap is unsigned int * at byte 44 — which is where both the header sizes and the sample strides below come from. Nothing is decoded, scaled or swizzled on the way in.
This is a different format from I.G.I. 1 terrain rather than a later version of it, so it is a separate reader; see and for the first game, whose grids are id-indexed records inside one file.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Formats.World.Igi2TerrainMap.Trailing
member.summary: Gets whatever follows the declared extent; empty for all but two retail files.

remarks.para: The original reads exactly nWidth * nHeight samples and never checks the file length, so a longer file loads and its tail is simply never addressed. Two shipped height maps are longer: location3/LEVEL4's heightmap000.thm and heightmap001.thm each carry 87,380 bytes past their 256×256 base — 128² + 64² + … + 1² samples, a complete mip pyramid. Comparing the first of those levels against a two-by-two box average of the base agrees to a mean absolute error of 3.8 over a value spread of 3.8 million, so it is a box-filtered mip chain and not coincidence.

It is exposed rather than dropped so that the bytes are visibly unused instead of invisibly discarded, but nothing reads it: the engine builds its own min and max height mip maps at run time into separate allocations (TerrainMap_AllocateMinMaxHeightMipMaps, igi2ed 0x6296B0), eight bytes per sample rather than four, so this tail is not what feeds them.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefAttachment
member.summary: One record of a model's ATTA chunk: a named point on the model that another object hangs off.

remarks.para: Attachments are how the world grows past what the level script places. 0x4DFA50 walks the attachments of a placed model, looks each up in the magic-object table that magicobj/magicobj.qvm fills through the DefineMagicObj native, and spawns a child object carrying that definition's model at this attachment's position and orientation. The child's own model is walked the same way, so the tree nests.
This is why a level-1 garage whose script node has no children at all still owns 67 baked lightmaps: three for its own LOD chain and 64 for the crates, doors and lamps its model attaches.

member.param: The magic-object type name, up to 16 bytes, NUL-padded on disk.
The attachment point in model space.
The attachment's rotation, stored row by row.
The trailing field, whose meaning is still open.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefCollisionMesh
member.summary: A model's collision geometry: the shape the world is solid with.

remarks.para: Four chunk groups, headed by HSMC. Its 64-byte payload holds two 32-byte MultiMesh_Mesh_t headers, one for each collision mesh level. A non-empty level has its own ECFC, XTVC, TAMC, and HPSC chunk, in level order. Every stride below was checked against the retail packs. The complete XTVC payload, not the HSMC header, is the authoritative vertex row count: a header that undercounts its rows is tolerated. No model in the fourteen retail missions' packs does (a full scan finds every header equal to its rows); the tolerance exists for a reported install whose human model declared fewer rows than it stored.

item.description: faces, 8 bytes: four u16
vertices, 16 bytes: three floats and a zero
materials, 12 bytes
spheres, 24 bytes: a centre, a radius, two dwords

remarks.para: The spheres are a binary tree over the faces. Their count is exactly 2 × faces − 1 in every model sampled — 40 faces to 79 spheres, 152 to 303, 1180 to 2359 — which is the node count of a binary tree with one leaf per face. The root's fifth dword carries 0xFFFF in its low half where the others carry small ascending indices, which is what a "no parent" marker looks like.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefDrawRecord
member.summary: One draw record from a model's DNER chunk: a run of triangles that share a material slot.

remarks.para: Records are packed back to back and fill the chunk exactly; there are as many as the render header's sub-mesh count. The header is 28 bytes for and models and 32 bytes for ones, followed by indexCount 16-bit indices.

Indices are relative to in every format. An earlier reading had the Diffuse and Skinned formats indexing the whole vertex array; measurement over mission 1's multi-record models (the truck 622_01_1 most visibly) showed every record's indices span exactly the run up to the next record's base. remains for the record's own bookkeeping.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefDrawRecord.IsTransparent
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the record is a transparent face group.
member.remarks: The word at offset 22 of the compact header. The model draw (0x49DF60) draws a record with it clear straight away, opaque and lit, and defers one with it set to the depth-sorted transparent pass (0x49EC70). A lightmapped record keeps it at offset 24 (0x49F1C0).

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefDrawRecord.IsAdditive
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether a transparent record is drawn additively.
member.remarks: Bit 0 of the byte at offset 24. The transparent pass (0x49EC70) then draws the texture alone -- lighting off, the texture colour selected, fog off -- at ONE, ONE; without it, lit, at SRCALPHA, INVSRCALPHA. The explosion FireBall (1006_01_1) is one such record: a flame painted on black that only reads added to the scene.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefDrawRecord.IsAlphaTested

member.remarks: I.G.I. 2's 0x40 in the face group's bMaterialProperties: Direct3DRender_DrawRigidFacegroup then draws it with the alpha-test blend state, which keeps texels of alpha 64 and over. Project I.G.I.'s records carry no such flag.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefLightmapPage
member.summary: One entry of a model's PMTL (LTMP) table: the size of a baked object-lightmap page.

remarks.para: The table has one entry per page and the render header's lightmap count agrees with it exactly for all 5628 lightmapped models in the retail corpus. A model's draw records each name the page they sample through .

The size is what the pixels in the matching .olm entry are: the original's lightmap builder (0x523D40) copies these two shorts straight into the image descriptor it writes, so a page and its baked image always agree. The remaining four bytes of the entry are zero in every retail model.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefMeshFormat.Diffuse
member.summary: 32-byte vertices (position, normal, one UV set). Draw-record indices are absolute. Batched into a shared vertex buffer by the original.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefMeshFormat.Skinned
member.summary: 40-byte vertices carrying a skin binding in place of the lightmap UV, drawn by the bone path. These are the animated models: the render header splits the array into base vertices and extra weighted influences, and each vertex names the bone that moves it.
member.remarks: Previously read as "the same layout as , just never batched". That was wrong: 0x49F700 takes the bone path on exactly this format, and the last eight bytes are { f32 weight, u16 targetVertex, u16 boneIndex }.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefMeshFormat.Lightmapped
member.summary: 40-byte vertices (position, normal, diffuse UV, lightmap UV) with a LTMP descriptor. Draw records carry a vertex span and their indices are relative to the record's base vertex.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefModel
member.summary: A static model loaded from a .mef file: an ILFF container of form type OCEM.

remarks.para: The original's Model_Load (0x4CF390) only walks the chunk list and back-patches pointers into the mesh header; the renderable geometry is parsed by the backend hook dword_A94E84[Backend_Id()] (0x49FB10 for the D3D backend). Both halves are done here, because OpenIGI's renderer is not the original's.
Collision, attachment and portal chunks are exposed as raw payloads: their record layouts are still open and are not needed to draw a level. See docs/formats/mef.md.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefModel.ReadFaceGroups(OpenIGI.Formats.Ilff.IlffContainer,OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefMeshFormat,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Reads I.G.I. 2's face-group table and the separate index chunk it points into.

remarks.para: The sequel keeps a flat array of fixed-size groups -- RigidDirect3D_FaceGroup_t at 32 bytes for the unskinned and skinned formats, LightmapDirect3D_FaceGroup_t at 28 for the lightmapped one -- and one index array in ECAF that every group names a run of. I.G.I. 1 instead packs each record's indices after its own header, which is why its reader varies the record length and this one does not.

Indices are absolute here, not relative to the group's start vertex. Confirmed twice: 5,486 of 7,535 groups sampled carry indices past their own vertex count, and the renderer binds the index buffer once per mesh before the group loop (Direct3DRender_DrawRigidMesh), so the base vertex it passes is that mesh's offset within a shared buffer rather than anything per group.

member.summary: A model's portals: the openings through which one sector can see into another.

remarks.para: Three chunks, whose layouts the sequel's symbols name in full — Mesh3D_Portal_t (20 bytes), Mesh3D_PortalFace_t (12) and Mesh3D_PortalVertex_t (12, a bare real32x3_t). The same chunks exist in Project I.G.I., which is why this lives in the shared format layer rather than in either title.

The first face's winding is the portal's facing. Sector_IsPortalVisible takes the cross product of that one triangle's edges as the plane normal and flips it toward the camera; the remaining faces only widen the outline.

A portal is not necessarily a quad, and not necessarily a triangle fan. Across I.G.I. 2's 794 placed portals the commonest shape is the quad (602 of them, four vertices and two triangles) but they run to 28 vertices and 22 triangles, and 41 have a face count that is not vertices - 2 — v28 f14 is seven separate quads, not one fan. So a reader that triangulated the vertex list itself, or assumed four corners, would be wrong on a quarter of them. Both counts are taken from the record.

is the portal's index within its own model, and it does two jobs. It indexes the per-object array of open/closed flags a door drives (PortalStatus_s, one byte), and it is what SectorObject_TraverseSector compares across objects: stepping through a portal admits every sector in the same sector container that has a portal with the same slot number. That is a coarser rule than a true portal graph — it pairs by authored slot rather than by geometry — but it is the rule the original follows.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefPortalSet.NormalOf(OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefPortal)
member.summary: Gets the outward normal of a portal, in the model's own space.
member.param: The portal.
member.returns: The unnormalised normal, or zero when the portal has no faces or is degenerate.

remarks.para: Taken from the first face alone, which is what Sector_IsPortalVisible does (igi2.exe 0x587D88–0x587E03); the remaining faces only widen the outline.

The sign is meaningful and this returns the original's. An earlier version of this method crossed the edges from vertex 1 rather than vertex 0, which for a triangle is exactly the negation, under a remark saying the sign did not matter because "the original flips it toward the camera at use". It does not. The sign is a test: the engine dots this against the direction from the camera, and only on the far side does it negate — locally, to project the camera onto the portal's plane and reject anything more than 409.6 units off it. A caller that took the opposite normal would apply that relief to exactly the portals that should skip it.

member.summary: Chunk HSEM (MESH): the mesh header.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefTags.ShadowMesh
member.summary: Chunk SEMS (SMES): the header of a shadow-volume mesh.

remarks.para: A shadow volume is a model in its own right rather than a broken one: it carries SMES/SVTX/SFAC/EDGE and no at all, because it is silhouette geometry to be extruded rather than a surface to be shaded.

The original loads it through a different function entirely. MTP_ShadowVolumeLoad (igi2ed 0x41FA00) opens LOCAL:models/<name>.mef and asks for exactly these four chunks — the header at 28 bytes a row (its count is the chunk size over 28), faces at 28, vertices at 12 and edges at 8 — while never touching the mesh reader. So a shadow volume sitting in a models archive is not something the model reader should be asked about at all.
Sixty-eight of them sit in the sequel's common pack — shadow_1, truckshade, Ftire_shade and their like — and reading each as a render model reported every one as malformed, once per file, every load.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MtpFile
member.summary: The raw chunk list of an .mtp resource pack: an EA IFF-85 FORM of type MTP .

remarks.para: Mirrors the original's walker at 0x4CEAA0: the first chunk sits at offset 12, chunk headers are eight bytes (tag then size), sizes are big-endian, and each payload is padded to a four-byte boundary. The bound is 8 + FORM.size, which equals the file length for every retail pack.
The endianness is mixed and this is the trap: only the IFF chunk sizes are big-endian. Every integer inside a payload is little-endian like the rest of the game's data.
Parsing is zero-copy; payloads are slices of the buffer passed to .
