member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.MtpMaterial
member.summary: One entry of a pack's GTT material table: a diffuse texture and a palette.

remarks.para: A model's draw record names a slot; the instance turns that slot into an index into this table; this table gives the two halves. MTP_ParseMTP (igi2.exe 0x4F5DE0) reads them as gtt[2 * slot] and gtt[2 * slot + 1] and resolves each against a table of its own.

is in every entry of every retail pack — all 12,523 of them, across both games. Object lightmaps are bound per object from lightmaps/lightmaps.res instead, and 8-bit palettised textures are not what either shipped game draws, so this field is only ever exercised by modified data.

The original resolves it against three different tables: −1 against paPalInfo, which indexes it at −1 and reads out of bounds; a level-local id against paPalInfoExtra; and a common-pack id against the common pack's paPalInfo. OpenIGI diverges on the first: "none" means no palette. No retail path reaches any of the three.

member.param: The diffuse texture id, in the pack's TEXF id space.
The palette id, or .

member.summary: Resolves the diffuse texture a draw record samples, all the way to its name.
member.param: The instance being drawn.
The slot from the model's draw record.
Receives the texture's bare name, without a path or an extension.
member.remarks:
The whole chain in one call — slot to GTT to TEXF — because both games walk it identically and a title that resolved it itself would be reimplementing 's other half.
A texture id addressing the common pack is refused rather than followed. The pack list a common id would be resolved against is the resource system's, not this type's, and no retail pack in either game ships one — GTT's texture half is the identity mapping throughout, so every id is below by construction. A caller that one day needs the common case has to supply the other pack, which is a signature this cannot have.

remarks.para: Entries are named <objectName>_<%05d>.olm (format string at 0x54F09C, used by 0x523D40), where the number is the index of the model's draw record the map belongs to. The original only loads them for models that have triangles.

An entry holds one or more images: a 60-byte prefix, then one 44-byte descriptor per image, then the pixel blocks in the same order. 25320 of the 25333 retail entries hold a single image, which is why a single 104-byte header appears to fit — it is the one-image case of 60 + 44*count. Twelve entries hold two images and one holds three.

member.summary: The size in bytes of one image descriptor in Project I.G.I.
member.remarks: I.G.I. 2's is 52. The size is what a caller supplies through ; this constant is kept so the I.G.I. 1 number has a name and so the minimum-length check has something to quote.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.World.ObjectLightmap.Read(System.ReadOnlyMemory{System.Byte},OpenIGI.Formats.AssetFormatProfile)
member.summary: Parses a lightmap.
member.param: The entry bytes.
The title's format policy, which supplies the descriptor stride.
member.exception: The bytes do not match the documented layout.

remarks.para: The two games differ by the descriptor only. A wrong stride is not a degraded read: the pixel blocks start at the wrong offset and every image after the first is noise, which is why the closing arithmetic below is an assertion rather than a courtesy.

Required, with no default. It used to default to the first game, and the shared world renderer took that default — so every I.G.I. 2 level drew unlit while its archive was there and readable, reporting one refused entry per object. A caller that does not know which game it is reading cannot pick a stride, and asking it to say so is the only thing that makes that visible at the call site rather than at the first frame.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Formats.World.ObjectLightmap.VariantLetters
member.summary: The letters an I.G.I. 2 entry name uses to separate one task's lightmap groups.
member.remarks: acIndexLetters (igi2ed 0x6CB554) is "!abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz". Index zero is the !, and it is never emitted: the writer takes the lettered format string only when the index is non-zero, so a is one, b is two, and a name with no letter is zero. The retail corpus uses a, b, c and e.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.World.ObjectLightmap.TryParseIgi2Name(System.String,System.Int32@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@,System.Int32@)
member.summary: Splits an I.G.I. 2 lightmap entry name into its four parts.
member.param: The entry name, with or without a directory prefix and with or without the extension.
Receives the level id of the task the lightmapped object belongs to.
Receives the group letter as a number, or zero when the name carries none.
Receives the index of the model within that task's enumeration.
Receives the level of detail, counted from one.
member.returns: when the name has the expected shape.

remarks.para: The sequel names lightmaps differently enough to need its own parser rather than a parameter. I.G.I. 1 writes <objectName>_<%05d>.olm, where the number indexes the model's draw records; I.G.I. 2 writes %04d_%04d_%1d.olm or %04d%c_%04d_%1d.olm (LightmapInfo_AddLightmapVirModelToEnumeration, igi2ed 0x625A20), where the parts are a task id, an optional group letter, a model index and a level of detail.

Reading the sequel's names with the first game's parser is the trap this exists to close: splitting on the last underscore succeeds, and hands back the level of detail where a draw-record index was expected.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainCommandBlock
member.summary: One chunk's block in terrain.cmd: a triangle strip, then the vertices it indexes.

remarks.para: The 8-byte header is {u16 triangleCount, s16 triangleBytes, u16 baseVertices, u16 extraVertices} and the block's size derives from it exactly — validated over 67907 blocks and 748303 triangles across thirteen levels, with no mismatches. sub_510010 reaches the vertices by adding triangleBytes to block + 8, which is what identifies the two trailing sections as the vertex stream rather than the per-pass attribute blocks an earlier reading assumed.
The block is a view over the file's bytes; nothing is copied until or is called.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainPackedVertex
member.summary: One vertex of a chunk, packed into a single dword of 6-bit fields.

remarks.para: The three coordinates are offsets from the chunk's centre in units of a twenty-fourth of the chunk's extent: ±24 spans the chunk's cube exactly, which is the check that pins the bias. No retail vertex exceeds that range.

A vertex past additionally carries the vertex it morphs from and two edge selectors, in the bits the base vertices leave unused. That is the seam morphing which lets two levels of detail meet without a crack.

member.param: The raw vertex dword.

member.summary: A terrain.cmd file: the geometry of every octree node, addressed by the byte offset each holds.

remarks.para: There is no directory and no block count — the file is only ever entered through an octree node's offset, which is why is the whole interface. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainGridTable
member.summary: The table both terrain.bit and terrain.hmp open with: 256 fixed records, then one variable-size block per record that declares a non-zero size.

remarks.para: Each record is {u32 data, u32 flags, u32 n}. data is a file offset the original back-patches into a pointer as it walks — it is meaningless on disk, and the blocks simply follow the table in record order. Only n and the ordering matter for reading, and the arithmetic closes byte-exactly for every retail file.

The record index is the id the renderer selects a grid by, and id 0 means "none": the original guards every lookup with a non-zero test, and its runtime expansion of these tables reuses record zero's storage for unrelated globals.
A file shorter than the table is not an error. The original allocates a zeroed table instead, so a level with a stub file behaves as though every record were empty.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainHeightmap
member.summary: A terrain.hmp file: up to 255 height grids, selected by id.

remarks.para: Seven of the fourteen retail levels ship no terrain.hmp at all. The original guards the load with a file-exists test and leaves the pointer null, so a heightmap is optional and a terrain without one is complete, not broken — the chunk geometry in terrain.cmd already carries the shape, and the heightmap only refines the finest levels of detail.

Which grid a chunk samples, and the origin and scale it samples at, are not in this file. They come from run-time bindings a level script's tasks publish (0xBA2030), which is why takes grid coordinates and leaves the mapping to its caller.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainHeightGrid.Sample(System.Double,System.Double)
member.summary: Samples the grid bilinearly and converts to engine units.
member.param: The column in grid coordinates; the fractional part interpolates.
The row in grid coordinates.
member.returns: The height in engine units, zero outside the grid.

remarks.para: The original truncates towards zero to reach the cell and interpolates in double, and this does the same.

The far edge — or exactly — is inside the grid: the row holds Size + 1 samples so that the cell's last column is covered, and the original reads it (its wrap-around neighbour is multiplied by a zero fraction). Treating it as outside opened a crack of the full height along every boundary between two cells, where the chunk on one side sampled its grid's last column as flat while the chunk on the other side sampled its own grid's first. Beyond that, a sample outside the grid reads as flat rather than wrapping: the original would read its neighbour's row, which is an artefact of the pointer arithmetic rather than intent, and no bound chunk reaches it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainLightmaps
member.summary: A terrain.lmp file: a flat sequence of square, 8-bit baked lightmap pages.

remarks.para: Each record is {u32 size; u8 texels[size * size]}. A size of zero is a hole and consumes only its four bytes, which matters: level 14 is 171 holes out of 172 records. Retail sizes are 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256, and the walk closes exactly for all fourteen levels.
Texels are indices, not intensities. The original expands them through a 256-entry ramp it builds in place as i << 16; the pages are kept 8-bit here so that expansion belongs to whoever uploads them.
Which page a chunk samples, and the planar mapping it samples with, come from a run-time binding a level script's tasks publish (0xBA80B0) rather than from this file.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainMaterial
member.summary: One terrain material, as the CreateTerrainMaterial script native declares it: a flag word and thirty-two bands, one per level-of-detail exponent.

remarks.para: The native takes 226 arguments and that number is the layout: 1 id, 1 flag word, and 32 × 7 band values. The original stores the record as 225 consecutive dwords at 0xC28FE0 + 900 * id and indexes a band by the drawn chunk's exponent, so a material describes how a ground type is textured at every distance rather than at one.

Every retail level registers materials 0 to 6. In level 1's material 0 only the two tile-map ids vary across the bands — (0,0) eight times, then (0,1), (1,1) twice, (1,2), and (2,2) for the remaining twenty — which is a coarse-to-fine progression.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainMaterial.Flags
member.summary: Gets the flag word, which is really the game material this ground is made of.

remarks.para: Argument 1 is not a flag word — it is an index into the game material table. 0x4CB810 answers "what is underfoot here" by taking the low byte of this very field (LOBYTE(materials[225 * id]), the row's first dword) and using it to select scene+3388+4·index — the same per-level array a mesh face's own 16-bit material index selects in 0x4C1840. The terrain leaf query then writes the result to offset 76 of its hit block, which becomes Human+1772: the field the footstep handler and both landings read.

The retail values say the same thing plainly. Every terrain material in a level declares one value, and there are only two across the campaign: 1 in levels 1–6, 9, 10, 13 and 14, and 20 in the four snow missions, 7, 8, 11 and 12. Against material.qvm's row order those are Ground and Snow — so walking on the ground outdoors is meant to sound like earth in most of the game and like snow in the Arctic ones.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainNode
member.summary: One 32-byte record of a terrain.ctr file: a node of the terrain octree.

remarks.para: The layout, from the descent in sub_4D14E0:

item.description: u16 × 8 — the child record indices, one per slot.
u8 × 8 — the child orientations; see .
u8 — which of the eight slots are occupied.
constant across a whole level; meaning open.
always zero.
u32 — the byte offset of this node's block in terrain.cmd.

remarks.para: A node carries geometry whether or not it has children: the octree is a level-of-detail hierarchy, so a coarse node draws a coarse version of everything beneath it. That is why the descent stops as soon as a node is detailed enough rather than always running to a leaf.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainOctree
member.summary: A terrain.ctr file: the octree the terrain renderer descends, one 32-byte per record.

remarks.para: The tree covers a cube of ± engine units about the world origin. It is not a coordinate table: a node's position is accumulated during the descent, halving the octant offset at each step, which is why nothing in the file looks like a position.
The root is record 1, not record 0 — sub_4D14E0 starts at ctr + 32. Record 0 is never entered.

Because children carry an orientation, one record can serve as many different subtrees; over the retail corpus a record is referenced about six times on average. Consumers must therefore key anything they cache on the node's position, never on its record index.

member.remarks: A node at level-of-detail exponent e spans RootExtent >> e about its centre, so the root itself is exponent zero.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainOrientation
member.summary: The eight orientations a terrain octree node can be authored in — the symmetry group of the square, acting on the X and Y octant axes only.

remarks.para: A .ctr record stores, per child, both a record index and an orientation byte (+16). The orientation lets one authored subtree be reused at eight different rotations, which is why the eight u16s reference every record in the file several times over: the octree is a DAG, not a tree.
The group shows up three times in the original and this type is where all three meet:

list.item: the composition table at 0xB12BE0, filled at run time by sub_4D0EF0, which the descent uses to fold a child's orientation into its parent's — see ;
the flag bits sub_510010 applies to a chunk's packed vertices — see .

remarks.para: All three agree, which is the check RetailTerrainGoldenTests makes: the index is rotation | (reflection << 2), quarter turns counted the same way in each.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainOrientation.Compose(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Folds a child's stored orientation into its parent's, giving the child's orientation.
member.param: The orientation the descent reached the parent with.
The byte at .ctr + 16 + slot.
member.returns: The orientation to descend into the child with.
member.remarks: This is the closed form of the table sub_4D0EF0 builds at 0xB12BE0, and it composes the two the way the descent needs: the parent's mapping runs first, so Slots[Compose(a, b)][i] == Slots[b][Slots[a][i]]. A reflection reverses the sense of the rotation that follows it, which is where the subtraction comes from.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainTileMap
member.summary: One tile map, as the CreateTerrainTileMap script native declares it: an 8×8 grid of tile indices into the level's terrain.tex atlas.

remarks.para: The native takes 65 arguments — an id and 64 tiles — and the original writes them straight to 0xC30080 + 64 * id. The renderer indexes the grid with three bits of the tiled texture coordinate in each axis, which is what makes it 8×8 rather than a flat list.

Every retail level registers maps 0 to 7, except level 8 which stops at 6. They are visibly patterns rather than data: level 1's map 0 is all zeros, map 2 alternates 3,4 over 5,6 in 2×2 blocks, and map 7 alternates 16,17 per column.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainVisibility
member.summary: A terrain.bit file: up to 255 one-bit-per-cell masks, selected by id.

remarks.para: It shares its 256-record table with ; only the block size differs, at one bit rather than one byte per cell. Every retail level ships one and all fourteen walk exactly.

The renderer samples these to decide which terrain material covers a vertex — a chunk is drawn once per material its vertices select, which is how two ground types blend across one chunk. The mapping from world position to cell comes from a run-time binding a level script publishes (0xBA5050), not from this file, so this type exposes the grids and leaves that to its caller.
